Difference in differences with two-way fixed effects

Source: R/didfe.R
didfe.Rd

The effect of a policy on a unit-by-period panel (towns by year, beats by month, courts by quarter) from a regression of the outcome on the treatment with unit and period fixed effects, with standard errors clustered by unit or by any coarser grouping, one-way or two-way. Counts can be fitted by Poisson or negative binomial regression with the same effects. Options give the estimate leaving out each treated unit in turn, its Goodman-Bacon decomposition, and the estimate after matching treated units to comparison units on their outcomes before treatment.

Usage

didfe(
  y,
  unit,
  time,
  trt,
  adj = NULL,
  clus = NULL,
  w = NULL,
  fe = "both",
  fam = "ols",
  expo = NULL,
  loo = FALSE,
  bacon = FALSE,
  mtch = 0,
  exact = NULL,
  calip = NULL,
  level = 0.95
)

Arguments

y

The outcome: finite numbers, one per row (counts from 0 for fam = "pois" or "nb").

unit

The unit of each row: labels.

time

The period of each row: numbers (a year, a month index); each unit at most once per period.

trt

The treatment of each row: 0 or 1 (or FALSE or TRUE).

adj

NULL or time-varying controls: a data frame or list of columns, a numeric matrix, or one vector, one value per row. Factor, text and logical columns enter as indicators of each level but the first.

clus

NULL (cluster by unit), the cluster of each row (labels), or a list or data frame of two such columns for two-way clustering.

w

NULL or weights from 0, one per row (population, matching weights); rows of weight 0 take no part.

fe

"both" (unit and period effects) or "time" (period effects only).

fam

"ols" (least squares), "pois" (Poisson) or "nb" (negative binomial) regression.

expo

NULL or the exposure of each row for counts (population, person-days): positive numbers; its logarithm is the offset.

loo

TRUE for the estimate leaving out each ever-treated unit in turn.

bacon

TRUE for the Goodman-Bacon decomposition.

mtch

0, or the number of comparison units matched to each treated unit before the fit.

exact

NULL or labels, constant within units: match only within them (a region, a district).

calip

NULL or the largest distance of a match, in standard deviations of the distances.

level

The confidence level of the intervals: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

Value

An object of class didfe, a list: coef, one row per term (the treatment "trt" first, then the controls): term, est, se, lo, hi, stat (t or z), p, and for counts rr, rrlo, rrhi; fit, one row: n (rows used), units, periods, ncl (G), k (K), ctlmean, releff, theta (negative binomial), dropped (units with no counts); vcov, the variance of the terms; loo (unit, est, se), bacon (type, treated, control, est, weight; control is Inf for the never treated) and match (treated, control, dist), each NULL unless asked for; fam; and level.

Details

The model is y_it = b trt_it + adj_it'g + a_i + m_t + e_it, fitted by least squares after the within transformation (alternating projections, so an unbalanced panel is fine; weights w give weighted least squares with weighted means). With fe = "time" the unit effects are left out. The variance is the cluster-robust CR1 estimator, G / (G - 1) (n - 1) / (n - K) times the sandwich, K counting the regressors, the constant, and the levels less one of each fixed effect not nested in a cluster; with two kinds of cluster it is V1 + V2 - V12 (Cameron, Gelbach and Miller 2011) with G the smaller number of clusters. Tests and intervals use Student's t on G - 1 degrees of freedom. These are the conventions of 'fixest' and Stata's 'reghdfe'. Fewer than ten clusters give a warning: wcbx() is the tool for so few.

With fam = "pois" or "nb" the model is E(y_it) = exp(b trt_it + adj_it'g + a_i + m_t) times the exposure expo, fitted by maximum likelihood with dummies for the effects (the steps of cntreg()). Units and periods whose counts are all zero carry nothing about b and are dropped first. The Poisson estimate is consistent whatever the dispersion (Wooldridge 1999); the sandwich and its factor are those of the least-squares fit, and intervals are normal; rr is the rate ratio exp(b). With unit dummies the negative binomial is the unconditional fixed-effects model, which behaves well when there are many periods per unit (Allison and Waterman 2002).

releff is the estimate over ctlmean, the mean outcome of the units never treated before the first treatment (the untreated rows before it when every unit is treated at some point): "a 12% fall". For counts it is rr - 1.

With bacon = TRUE (a balanced panel, treatment that stays on, no adjustment or weights), the estimate is split into the two-group, two-period comparisons it averages, with their weights (Goodman-Bacon 2021, theorem 1): treated against never treated, earlier against later treated before the later start, and later against earlier treated after the earlier start (already-treated units as controls). The weights sum to 1 and sum(weight * est) is the estimate exactly. Units treated from the first period act as an already-treated group.

With mtch a whole number above 0, each treated unit is matched, with replacement, to its mtch nearest units never treated by the Mahalanobis distance of their outcomes in every period before the first adoption, with the pooled within-group covariance (as 'MatchIt' computes it), within its exact group and, with calip, within calip standard deviations of all the distances computed. A comparison unit's weight is the sum, over the treated units it serves, of one over their number of matches; matched treated units weigh 1 and the rest 0. The estimate is then the weighted fit. Matching on the outcomes before treatment can bring in regression to the mean when units were chosen for an unusual pre-period (Daw and Hatfield 2018).

References

Bertrand, M., Duflo, E. and Mullainathan, S. (2004). How much should we trust differences-in-differences estimates? Quarterly Journal of Economics, 119(1), 249-275. doi:10.1162/003355304772839588

Cameron, A. C., Gelbach, J. B. and Miller, D. L. (2011). Robust inference with multiway clustering. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 29(2), 238-249. doi:10.1198/jbes.2010.07136

Goodman-Bacon, A. (2021). Difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing. Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 254-277. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2021.03.014

Wooldridge, J. M. (1999). Distribution-free estimation of some nonlinear panel data models. Journal of Econometrics, 90(1), 77-97. doi:10.1016/S0304-4076(98)00033-5

Allison, P. D. and Waterman, R. P. (2002). Fixed-effects negative binomial regression models. Sociological Methodology, 32, 247-265. doi:10.1111/1467-9531.00117

Daw, J. R. and Hatfield, L. A. (2018). Matching and regression to the mean in difference-in-differences analysis. Health Services Research, 53(6), 4138-4156. doi:10.1111/1475-6773.12993

Examples

# twelve towns over ten years; four adopt a by-law in 2019, four in 2021
d <- expand.grid(year = 2015:2024, town = LETTERS[1:12])
i <- match(d$town, LETTERS)
first <- c(2019, 2019, 2019, 2019, 2021, 2021, 2021, 2021, NA, NA, NA, NA)
d$bylaw <- as.integer(!is.na(first[i]) & d$year >= first[i])
d$rate <- 30 + i + 0.5 * (d$year - 2015) - 4 * d$bylaw + sin(seq_len(120))
r <- didfe(d$rate, d$town, d$year, d$bylaw)
r
#> didfe: ols, 120 rows, 12 units, 10 periods, 12 clusters
#>  term       est        se       lo        hi      stat            p
#>   trt -4.179346 0.2529069 -4.73599 -3.622702 -16.52524 4.095738e-09
#> comparison mean 41.26246, relative effect -0.1012869
# its comparisons, and each adopting town left out in turn
didfe(d$rate, d$town, d$year, d$bylaw, bacon = TRUE, loo = TRUE)$bacon
#>               type treated control       est weight
#> 1 treated vs never    2019     Inf -4.081194  0.375
#> 2 treated vs never    2021     Inf -4.029237  0.375
#> 3 earlier vs later    2019    2021 -4.561454  0.125
#> 4 later vs earlier    2021    2019 -4.542020  0.125
